paragraphs: Learning a nonlinear dynamical system involves finding a representation of its changing state and a rule describing how that state evolves. This paper presents a subspace method that handles these tasks in sequence. Its foundation is stochastic realization, which provides the setting for constructing state representations from the observed dynamics.

The method first chooses state vectors using kernel canonical correlation analysis. These vectors supply the intermediate representation used in the next stage, where regression identifies the state-space system. The kernel component supports nonlinear identification, while the separation into state selection and regression gives the procedure a concrete computational structure.

The authors develop theoretical foundations and turn them into an algorithm that requires no iterative optimization procedure. They state that it can use fast, reliable numerical schemes, making its computational organization a central contribution. A simulation shows that the resulting model can represent dynamics accurately. That finding supports the approach in the simulated setting, alongside the theoretical and algorithmic developments.
neurips-2006-a-kernel-subspace-method-by.tldr: A kernel-based method learns nonlinear dynamical systems by selecting state vectors and fitting regressions without iterative optimization.

paragraphs: A time histogram estimates how a neuron's spike rate changes by collecting spikes into time bins. The width of those bins determines the time resolution and strongly affects how faithfully the histogram represents the underlying rate. This paper replaces an informal researcher choice with an objective selection method based on the recorded spikes.

The method selects a bin size intended to best approximate the unknown rate. Its analysis connects achievable resolution to the amount of data: more sampled spike sequences permit smaller optimal bins. This makes the time scale visible in a histogram a question of what the observations support, rather than simply how finely someone chooses to plot them.

A particularly consequential result concerns too few trials from a moderately fluctuating rate process. In that case, the optimal bin size can diverge, signaling that attempts to characterize the changing rate would produce spurious results. The method can also suggest how many additional trials are needed to reach a requested resolution, connecting analysis choices directly to experimental planning.
neurips-2006-a-recipe-for-optimizing-a-t.tldr: An objective histogram rule selects time-bin widths from spike data and can indicate when more trials are needed.

paragraphs: Selective attention helps sensory systems cope with limited capacity by processing salient parts of an input in sequence while suppressing less salient regions. This paper develops a hardware building block for modeling that behavior. The goal is to make attention operate within a physical neuromorphic system that processes sensory input through spikes.

The implementation combines analog and digital circuitry on a very large scale integration chip. The paper describes the chip's architecture and examines its behavior as part of a system containing multiple chips. Input comes from a spiking retina, so the attention component is considered together with an event-producing sensory front end.

The authors show how this arrangement can implement flexible models of bottom-up attention in real time. Here, attention is driven by the sensory input's salience. The contribution therefore connects an account of selective sensory processing to a working hardware arrangement, showing how a chip can serve as a reusable component in a larger attention system.
neurips-2006-a-selective-attention-multi.tldr: A mixed analog/digital chip supports real-time models of bottom-up attention in a multichip system receiving spiking-retina input.

paragraphs: EEG brain-computer interfaces need features that distinguish mental states despite interference in the recordings. Common Spatial Patterns, or CSP, can classify imagined limb movements well, but the paper identifies its dependence on artifact-free training data as a robustness problem. The proposed alternative uses prior knowledge about where the relevant brain activity originates.

The adaptive filter maximizes the variance attributed to a predefined brain region relative to the total variance in the measured EEG. This directs the filter toward a chosen source region. For imagined hand movements, the authors use the known involvement of the motor cortex and construct separate filters centered on its left and right hand areas.

The filters are evaluated on recordings from three subjects imagining right- and left-hand movements. They outperform CSP in that evaluation and achieve classification rates up to 94.7% without rejecting artifacts. The result demonstrates how anatomical prior information can support useful classification in recordings where the usual requirement for clean training data is problematic.
neurips-2006-adaptive-spatial-filters-wi.tldr: Spatial filters guided by motor-cortex locations outperform CSP on three subjects' imagined-hand-movement EEG without artifact rejection.

paragraphs: Estimating motion is difficult when objects have clear outlines but little visible texture. Corners can help resolve movement, yet apparent features such as T-junctions can suggest misleading motion. The paper explains that local covariance information alone cannot reliably distinguish real features from these spurious ones, motivating an approach that avoids relying on such points.

The method combines three levels of boundary information: small oriented edge elements, chains of those elements called boundary fragments, and complete contours. It estimates fragment motion from local evidence, then resolves uncertainty by grouping fragments into contours. Thus, interpreting which boundary pieces belong together helps determine how they move.

Grouping uses a graphical model whose uncertainty is handled through importance sampling. Two equivalent representations, based on switches at fragment ends and on fragment chains, capture local and global boundary statistics. Tests on synthetic and real video with strong boundaries and textureless regions produce good motion estimates alongside grouped and completed contours. The results support jointly reasoning about boundary organization and movement.
neurips-2006-analysis-of-contour-motions.tldr: A contour-based motion method resolves ambiguous local movement by grouping boundary fragments into coherent contours.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised support vector machines use both labeled and unlabeled examples to seek a wide-margin boundary through low-density parts of the data. Their optimization problem is nonconvex, so an implementation can settle at a local minimum. This creates a practical question: does poor performance reflect the learning objective or difficulty optimizing it?

The paper addresses that question with branch and bound, obtaining exact, globally optimal solutions. Solving the objective globally lets the authors examine what the model can achieve when local minima are removed from the explanation. The approach therefore serves as a way to investigate the potential of semi-supervised SVMs themselves.

The reported empirical evidence suggests that global solutions can generalize extremely well in situations where other implementations fail completely. This is a qualified finding about particular situations, rather than a guarantee that global optimization always gives good predictions. The current implementation handles only small datasets. The authors discuss variants that could potentially turn this diagnostic approach into practically useful algorithms.
neurips-2006-branch-and-bound-for-semi-s.tldr: Exact optimization reveals that semi-supervised SVMs can perform well where local-search implementations fail, although the implementation handles only small datasets.

paragraphs: Combining sensory information requires deciding whether different cues describe the same underlying event. If two cues share a cause, they should contribute to a joint estimate. If their causes differ, they should be processed independently. The paper studies the common situation in which a person does not know which causal interpretation is correct.

The authors formulate this uncertainty as a Bayesian estimation problem. Cue combination then depends on an inference about the relationship between the cues, alongside the information each cue provides. This extends the usual account in which several modalities are assumed to measure one shared variable and the main task is to combine their measurements.

The resulting model explains some experiments involving visual and auditory cues and some involving vision and proprioception, the sense of body position. The analysis suggests that producing movement from sensory evidence involves inferring the causal organization behind that evidence. Its significance is to make uncertainty about shared versus separate causes an explicit part of sensorimotor integration.
neurips-2006-causal-inference-in-sensori.tldr: A Bayesian model explains sensory cue combination by accounting for uncertainty about whether cues share a common cause.

paragraphs: Cooperative competitive networks combine interactions that strengthen some activity patterns and suppress others. This paper implements such a network with spiking neurons in VLSI hardware. It investigates context-dependent computation in two different aspects of the spikes: how frequently neurons fire and how closely their firing events are correlated in time.

For average firing rates, the network strengthens activity associated with a selected stimulus and suppresses neurons receiving weaker stimuli. This provides a form of selection expressed through the amount of activity. The experimental demonstration connects the network's cooperative and competitive organization to a measurable response to competing inputs.

The timing result concerns a different signal property. Through recurrent interactions, the network gives greater amplification to correlations among neurons receiving highly correlated inputs, while leaving the mean firing rate unchanged. The authors describe the architecture and present experimental evidence for both behaviors. Together, the findings show that context-dependent processing in this hardware can operate through either firing rates or relationships among spike times.
neurips-2006-context-dependent-amplifica.tldr: A spiking hardware network selectively amplifies firing rates or spike-time correlations, with correlation amplification leaving mean rates unchanged.

paragraphs: Classification can draw on several datasets that describe the same prediction problem in different ways. This paper presents a fully Bayesian approach to integrating such data, including potentially heterogeneous sources. Gaussian process priors provide the modeling framework, allowing the combination of information sources to be addressed within a single probabilistic treatment.

The integration operates through covariance functions, which encode relationships used by the Gaussian process. The approach infers how these functions should be combined. Because the required inference is approximate, the authors develop methods based on variational inference and expectation propagation and rigorously assess them as part of the proposed solution.

The application is a large-scale protein fold prediction problem involving multiple datasets. The authors report state-of-the-art performance while inferring optimal covariance-function combinations, without ad hoc parameter tuning or classifier combination. This result supports the value of learning how information sources fit together within the model. The contribution includes both the Bayesian formulation of integration and practical inference procedures for using it.
neurips-2006-data-integration-for-classi.tldr: A Bayesian Gaussian process framework learns how to combine heterogeneous datasets and reports state-of-the-art protein fold prediction.

paragraphs: Some objects are naturally described by a collection of measurements rather than a single observation. A movie may have many user ratings, and a sensor may produce a time series. This paper studies clustering when each object is represented by a multivariate Gaussian distribution fitted to such repeated measurements.

Each representation contains a mean vector and a covariance matrix. The mean describes the center of the measurements, while the covariance describes their variability and relationships. Treating this whole distribution as the input lets the clustering problem retain both aspects of an object, instead of reducing its description to a single representative point.

The authors formulate clustering through an information-theoretic approach and establish connections to Bregman divergences, including their matrix versions. These connections provide a mathematical account of comparing and organizing Gaussian representations. They evaluate the method on synthetic data, sensor-network data, and a statistical debugging application. These evaluations explore the framework across several settings where distributions are meaningful descriptions of individual inputs.
neurips-2006-differential-entropic-clust.tldr: An information-theoretic clustering method groups objects represented by Gaussian means and covariances rather than individual observations.

paragraphs: This paper learns sparse, overcomplete features without labels using an energy-based encoder–decoder model. A linear encoder produces a code estimate, while a sparsifying nonlinearity converts a code into a nearly binary sparse representation before linear decoding. The desired code balances reconstructing the input patch with staying close to the encoder's output.

Training alternates between two steps resembling expectation maximization. First, it finds a code that minimizes the energy; then it changes the encoder and decoder parameters to reduce that energy. This couples representation inference with learning a direct encoding function. The authors report fast inference and learning without preprocessing or expensive sampling.

Training on handwritten numerals produces stroke detectors, while natural-image patches produce Gabor-like filters. Using the method to initialize the first layer of a convolutional network yields an MNIST error rate slightly below the best previously reported result. The paper also describes an extension for learning topographical filter maps. These findings connect the learned representations to both recognizable image structure and a downstream classification application.
neurips-2006-efficient-learning-of-spars.tldr: An energy-based encoder–decoder learns sparse image features efficiently and provides useful initialization for a convolutional classifier.

paragraphs: Kernel-based learning balances fitting training observations against controlling model complexity. The representer theorem expresses the resulting solution using combinations of kernel functions anchored at data points. This paper extends that framework so that predefined features can participate in the same model, bringing supplied feature structure into kernel-based regularized learning.

The authors construct kernels that map both the predefined features and kernel translates into a common hypothesis space. They then introduce a generalized regularizer that leaves part of that space unpenalized. This allows different parts of the model to receive different treatment when complexity is controlled, while retaining a unified learning formulation.

With squared prediction error as the loss, the formulation yields a simple convex solution combining predefined features and kernel translates. The generalized representer theorem provides the theoretical support for that solution. Empirical evaluations confirm effectiveness on supervised learning tasks. The contribution is therefore a principled way to include predefined features within regularized kernel learning, together with an algorithm whose optimization remains convex.
neurips-2006-generalized-regularized-lea.tldr: A generalized representer theorem supports convex least-squares learning that combines predefined features with kernel functions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover the graph of a discrete Markov random field from observations. It estimates each node's neighborhood using logistic regression with an l1 constraint. The neighborhood estimates identify which other nodes are connected to each node, turning graph recovery into a collection of constrained regression problems.

The analysis allows both the number of nodes, p, and the largest neighborhood size, d, to increase with the number of observations, n. Its main result gives sufficient conditions for consistently recovering every neighborhood simultaneously. This addresses an entire growing graph, rather than guaranteeing accuracy only for one selected node.

Under mutual incoherence conditions, the authors show consistency when n grows faster than 6 d^6 log d + 2 d^5 log p. The logarithmic dependence on p is favorable, but the expression also has a substantial dependence on neighborhood size. Thus, the result establishes conditional sample sufficiency, with graph size and connectivity playing distinct roles. It does not establish that this observation count is necessary.
neurips-2006-high-dimensional-graphical-.tldr: Constrained logistic regressions can consistently recover a growing graph under stated incoherence and sample-growth conditions.

paragraphs: The paper reconstructs a surface from sample points and their normal vectors, which describe local surface orientation. It represents the surface implicitly: a function is learned, and the locations where that function equals zero form the surface. The central issue is how to construct and regularize this function using the supplied geometric evidence.

The authors introduce a way to regularize compactly supported basis functions at multiple scales. Such functions act within limited regions, yet the proposed regularization gives them desirable properties previously associated with fully supported bases. They also establish equivalence to a Gaussian process with a modified covariance function, linking the construction to a probabilistic representation.

A further regularization framework handles surface normals more directly and is supported by a generalized representer theorem. This integrates information about surface orientation into the mathematical treatment of reconstruction. Demonstrations include three-dimensional problems with up to 14 million data points and four-dimensional time-series data. These examples show the techniques applied to large geometric datasets and to data with a temporal component.
neurips-2006-implicit-surfaces-with-glob.tldr: A regularization framework reconstructs implicit surfaces using local basis functions, surface normals, and a Gaussian process connection.

paragraphs: Human similarity judgments are often pictured as distances between items in an internal geometric space. Evidence about whether such a metric representation is appropriate has been conflicting. This paper examines how a set of judgments that fits a Euclidean representation can become incompatible with that representation through the addition of a carefully constructed stimulus.

In a psychophysical experiment, the authors show that one influential judgment can introduce violations of Euclidean, or l2, geometry. They call this a conflictual judgment. Its importance lies in the contrast between its small share of the observations and its effect on whether the full collection admits the geometric description.

The paper also provides an algorithm for analyzing these data and identifying the crucial point. The findings suggest that metric and nonmetric representations need not form a strict either-or distinction. Large subsets of stimuli may still have a suitable metric representation even when a small subset makes the full set violate metricity. This offers a more localized way to interpret conflicting similarity evidence.
neurips-2006-inducing-metric-violations-.tldr: A carefully constructed stimulus can disrupt Euclidean similarity judgments even when a large subset remains compatible with metric representation.

paragraphs: Timestamped events and counts describe how activity changes over time, but different days can follow different patterns. This paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian framework for learning collections of such patterns. It represents activity through intensity functions that describe how frequently events occur across a time period.

A Dirichlet process framework learns categories and their associated intensity functions. These functions form a basis for representing individual periods according to their category assignments. The model can therefore discover recurring differences, such as weekday versus weekend behavior, as well as unusual effects associated with a single day.

An important part of the formulation is sharing information when periods belong to relevant categories. Shared evidence can improve estimates of category-specific behavior while the representation still accommodates distinctive occurrences. The authors illustrate the technique with real count datasets involving vehicles and people. The contribution is a data-driven way to organize temporal activity into reusable patterns and period-specific effects, rather than requiring those patterns to be fully specified beforehand.
neurips-2006-learning-time-intensity-pro.tldr: A Dirichlet process model learns recurring and day-specific activity profiles while sharing information across related time periods.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms could benefit from multiple processors, but implementing a separate parallelization strategy for each algorithm creates repeated work. This paper develops a common programming method for multicore machines. Its central contribution is identifying a computational structure shared by a broad class of learning algorithms.

The authors show that algorithms fitting the Statistical Query model can be expressed in a particular summation form. That structure allows work to be divided across processors and the resulting contributions to be combined. They adapt the map-reduce paradigm to turn this observation into a reusable approach to parallel machine learning.

Demonstrations cover algorithms including logistic regression, k-means, naive Bayes, SVMs, PCA, EM, and neural-network backpropagation. Across their experiments, the authors report approximately linear speedup as processor counts increase. This supports the practical value of the shared formulation for the tested settings. The theoretical applicability rests on the Statistical Query connection, while the reported scaling provides empirical evidence that one framework can accelerate several different learning procedures.
neurips-2006-map-reduce-for-machine-lear.tldr: A shared summation form enables map-reduce parallelization of many learning algorithms, with approximately linear speedups in experiments.

paragraphs: A single training example can contain several meaningful parts and belong to several categories. An image, for instance, can be represented by feature vectors for multiple patches while supporting more than one scene label. This paper formalizes a learning setting that accommodates both kinds of multiplicity together.

The proposed multi-instance multi-label framework assigns multiple instances and multiple class labels to each example. The authors analyze how it relates to traditional supervised learning, multi-instance learning, and multi-label learning. This clarifies how internal structure within an example and multiple valid descriptions of that example can be treated in a common problem formulation.

The paper introduces two algorithms, MIMLBOOST and MIMLSVM, and reports good performance in scene classification. The application puts the formulation to use where image patches supply the instances and scene categories supply the labels. The contribution combines a definition of this learning problem with concrete algorithms, showing how a richer representation of both inputs and outputs can be used in a practical classification task.
neurips-2006-multi-instance-multi-label-.tldr: The paper formalizes learning from examples with multiple instances and labels and introduces two algorithms for scene classification.

paragraphs: Many computer-aided diagnosis datasets contain a few positive bags of instances alongside very many negative instances. This imbalance creates a particular multiple-instance learning problem, and the paper argues that existing methods are too computationally expensive for these datasets. It introduces CH, a framework based on learning a convex-hull representation of multiple instances.

CH can be used with any standard learning algorithm based on a separating hyperplane. The authors report that it is significantly faster than existing multiple-instance methods. For some compatible algorithms, the framework also guarantees a globally optimal solution. That guarantee is tied to those algorithms rather than asserted for every possible use of CH.

Experiments on two diagnosis applications show significantly improved diagnostic accuracy compared with both multiple-instance and traditional classifiers. The authors also evaluate standard, relatively balanced multiple-instance benchmarks, even though those differ from the intended setting. CH is competitive with the state of the art there. The results support a formulation designed around diagnostic data imbalance while showing usefulness beyond that original setting.
neurips-2006-multiple-instance-learning-.tldr: A convex-hull learning framework speeds up imbalanced multiple-instance diagnosis problems and improves accuracy in two applications.

paragraphs: Traffic-signal control often relies on hand-tuned policies with limited automatic adjustment. More sophisticated controllers can require detailed traffic models that existing sensors do not directly provide. This paper investigates learning signal-control policies directly from the observations available through deployed sensors, using policy-gradient reinforcement learning.

The learned policy maps sensor observations to traffic-control signals. The authors apply natural actor-critic learning and include a conventional policy-gradient method for comparison. This places the optimization at the level of the control policy itself, addressing the difficulty of obtaining the traffic model required by other approaches.

The work also extends natural actor-critic methods to distributed, online problems with an infinite time horizon. Those extensions accommodate learning and control that continue over time across distributed components. The trained controllers are described as theoretically compatible with the traffic system used in Sydney and many other cities. This is a compatibility claim about the proposed approach; the abstract does not report a real-world deployment or a quantified traffic improvement.
neurips-2006-natural-actor-critic-for-ro.tldr: Policy-gradient learning maps existing traffic-sensor observations directly to signals and extends natural actor-critic methods for ongoing distributed control.

paragraphs: Principal component methods seek a smaller representation that preserves variation in the data. Sparse PCA additionally limits how many original coordinates contribute to that representation. This paper studies a version in which the projection weights must also be nonnegative, so a new coordinate combines selected inputs without negative contributions.

The objective balances retaining projected variance with using only parts of the original coordinate set. In the proposed formulation, nonnegativity further promotes sparsity by enforcing a partition of original coordinates among the new axes. This gives the representation a structure in which different axes use different portions of the input coordinates.

The authors develop a simple, efficient iterative method of the coordinate-descent type. It converges to a local optimum of their optimization criterion, which is a specific convergence result rather than a global-optimality guarantee. They report good results on large real-world datasets. The approach is motivated by settings such as economics, bioinformatics, and computer vision, where nonnegative projection weights are a desirable property.
neurips-2006-nonnegative-sparse-pca-09e9.tldr: Nonnegative sparse PCA builds low-dimensional projections from selected input coordinates using an efficient method that converges locally.

paragraphs: A weighted majority vote combines predictions from several classifiers, while its associated Gibbs classifier selects a classifier according to the same weighting distribution. This paper develops PAC-Bayes bounds on the majority vote's prediction risk. The bounds use both the mean and the variance of the Gibbs classifier's error.

Accounting for variance makes it possible to certify stronger performance for the vote than the Gibbs risk alone might suggest. The authors show that their bounds can be smaller than the Gibbs classifier's risk. They can even approach zero while the Gibbs risk remains close to one-half, demonstrating a possible large gap between these two quantities.

The paper also shows that the bounds can be estimated from training data uniformly over every posterior weighting distribution Q. This matters because the guarantee covers the choice of weights rather than requiring one fixed choice in advance. A large unlabeled sample can further improve the bounds. These are theoretical possibilities established by the analysis, not claims that every ensemble achieves near-zero risk.
neurips-2006-pac-bayes-bounds-for-the-ri.tldr: PAC-Bayes bounds using error mean and variance can certify low majority-vote risk even when Gibbs risk is near one-half.

paragraphs: Adaptive neurophysiology experiments choose stimuli to learn about a neural-response model efficiently. The computational obstacle is selecting the most informative stimulus quickly when both stimuli and model parameters have many dimensions. This paper develops an algorithm that makes this choice practical using an approximation to the information gained from an experiment.

The method combines a Fisher approximation of Shannon information with specialized numerical linear algebra. Stimulus selection requires low-rank matrix operations and a one-dimensional line search, reducing the computational burden of the high-dimensional problem. The authors report optimizing a 100-dimensional stimulus in 15 milliseconds on a desktop computer, supporting real-time use.

Simulations show that adaptive stimulus choices estimate model parameters much more efficiently than random, nonadaptive choices. The authors also extend the algorithm to account for rapid adaptation caused by spike history and slower, nonsystematic parameter drift. Together, these contributions address both the speed of experimental decisions and changes in neural responses, while the reported estimation advantage comes from simulation results.
neurips-2006-real-time-adaptive-informat.tldr: An information-approximation algorithm selects high-dimensional stimuli in real time and improves parameter estimation over random stimuli in simulations.

paragraphs: Relational learning predicts interactions between entities, such as preferences linking users and movies. This paper introduces stochastic relational models, a Gaussian process framework for predicting whether relationships exist, how strong they are, or what types they have. It uses a partially observed network and can also incorporate entity attributes when available.

The model combines Gaussian processes defined on different entity types through a tensor interaction. Each entry in the resulting relational representation corresponds to a relationship among a tuple of entities. This supplies nonparametric priors over potentially infinite-dimensional relational structures, allowing the model to express dependencies across linked entities.

Learning maximizes marginalized likelihood so that information passes between the participating Gaussian processes through the network. Relationship patterns influence the adapted kernels, connecting learned entity dependencies to observed links. The authors derive an efficient learning algorithm, discuss variants, and report encouraging results on a toy problem and a user–movie preference task. They also discuss extensions to broader relational learning problems.
neurips-2006-stochastic-relational-model.tldr: Stochastic relational models combine interacting Gaussian processes to predict links while adapting entity relationships from the observed network.

paragraphs: Finding the highest-probability assignment in a Markov random field is generally intractable, but some structured cases have efficient combinatorial solutions. Matching constraints and certain regular potentials are examples. The difficulty addressed here arises when those tractable structures appear inside a larger network containing other potentials that do not meet the same requirements.

The proposed COMPOSE method uses combinatorial optimization inside max-product belief propagation. It computes exact max-marginals for a whole tractable subnetwork, summarizing the best achievable scores under particular variable assignments. Those summaries then participate in inference for the full network. The authors develop efficient procedures for both bipartite-matching and regular subnetworks.

Tests use synthetic networks and real image-correspondence problems that combine matching constraints with pairwise geometric constraints. Compared with a range of methods, COMPOSE shows improved convergence, shorter running time, and higher-scoring assignments. The reported advantage comes from transmitting information across larger structured parts of the network. Exact subnetwork computations support the overall inference procedure without establishing global exactness for the entire mixed network.
neurips-2006-using-combinatorial-optimiz.tldr: COMPOSE embeds exact combinatorial subnetwork computations within belief propagation, improving convergence, runtime, and assignment scores in experiments.
